Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 33: Files — byte ranges, positions, and object identity
Dr. Charles Dorner

1. A file name, a file object, and an open position differ
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Imagine opening a report, then another process renaming a different report over the original pathname. The same path text can now lead to a different object, while the already-open handle still identifies the object it opened. This distinction matters when validating metadata and then reading. A name is a lookup route, not permanent object identity. The file also has contents, metadata, and an open position, which are separate facts. A parser must know which byte range it wants and whether the chosen interface can seek there. We will separate those facts before building a record-address calculation.

DO
Give the rename scenario before discussing file APIs.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.004 · 33.1 Regular files

------------------------------------------------------------

2. Fixed records require format arithmetic
Problem and first experiment

SAY
Our new format model has an eight-byte header and twelve-byte records in a fifty-six-byte file. Removing the header leaves forty-eight bytes, so there are four records. Record index two begins at eight plus twice twelve, or byte thirty-two. The program prints four and thirty-two. It first checks for a short header and incomplete trailing records, then validates the selected index. This is arithmetic over a declared format, not a read from a real disk. The sequence matters because unsigned subtraction on a too-small file size would wrap. Prove a calculation's inputs before using it to locate bytes.

DO
Predict the record count and offset before Run.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.014 · Worked example — Record boundaries without overflow

------------------------------------------------------------

3. An endpoint may be a stream without seeking
Problem and first experiment

SAY
A regular file lets a program revisit byte one hundred without reading every earlier byte again. A pipe does not provide that ordinary seek operation; it delivers bytes as they become available. Both can be read through a descriptor, so sharing an interface does not mean sharing every capability. A read asking for a thousand bytes might return ten available bytes successfully. The next read may return more. Also distinguish this endpoint meaning of stream from the C library's FILE object, which adds buffering on top of an endpoint. Good APIs state the capabilities they require rather than assuming every input is a disk file.

DO
Compare a regular-file reader with input arriving gradually through a pipe.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.006 · 33.2 Streams

------------------------------------------------------------

4. An explicit offset can avoid disturbing shared position
Problem and first experiment

SAY
This Linux and POSIX demonstration creates its own temporary file containing ABCDE. After flushing the library writer, it sets the underlying position to one. pread asks for two bytes at offset two, so it obtains C and D. Querying the current offset still returns one. The output therefore says slice equals CD and position equals one. No existing user file is touched. The example intentionally finishes buffered output before its descriptor operations and closes the stream afterward. Positional reads help independent readers avoid a shared seek-and-read sequence, but they still need bounds checks, return-value checks, and a policy for concurrent file changes.

DO
Predict both the bytes and the untouched position.

SOURCE
Lecture demonstration for content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.010 · 33.4 File position

6. Where the simple approach fails
The chapter problem

SAY
A file size does not say where a logical record begins or whether its contents are valid for the format.

A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Treat an empty returned string as failure. A valid zero-length slice then becomes indistinguishable from rejection.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Represent the success state separately from its data. Test the boundary at exactly end and just beyond end.

7. Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
The chapter problem

SAY
The slice owns its returned characters, so it does not depend on the original string’s later lifetime. The checks use the valid input extent, not its allocation capacity. An optional empty string is a success, while an empty optional is rejection. Real file reads can also fail or return fewer bytes; this memory model isolates the bounds contract.

A plausible alternative: Line-based text is convenient for simple human-readable records; fixed-width or indexed formats support different access needs.

8. Chapter 33 — Files
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A file interface presents data through a persistent name, an open handle, or a stream-like endpoint. The operating system hides many device details, but the abstraction does not make every endpoint behave like a seekable array of bytes. Correct I/O code begins by identifying which guarantees the particular object provides. The Linux/POSIX examples distinguish a pathname , an underlying filesystem object, an open file description , and a process’s file descriptor . Those are related objects, not four names for the same thing. The distinction explains shared offsets, inherited descriptors, and why removing a pathname need not immediately invalidate an already-open handle. [ R47 , R13 ]

10. Regular files
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A regular file provides byte-oriented contents and metadata under filesystem rules. It usually supports seeking to a position and reading or writing there. Its logical size need not equal the amount of physical storage allocated, as sparse regions illustrate. A pathname is a route through a directory namespace, not a permanent guarantee about object identity. Another process can rename or replace an entry between separate pathname operations. When an operation must apply to the object already opened, use the descriptor and descriptor-relative interfaces where appropriate rather than reopening the name and assuming it still denotes the same object.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

DO

11. Streams
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A stream exposes an ordered flow of bytes or records according to its interface. Pipes and TCP sockets are byte streams that do not support arbitrary seeking. Data may arrive gradually, and a read can return fewer bytes than requested. The C standard-I/O concept of a stream adds buffering and library state through FILE* . That is another layer: a FILE* may wrap a regular file or another supported endpoint. Distinguish the endpoint’s capabilities from the library abstraction used to access it.

12. Random-access files
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Random access means that the program can select positions rather than consume data only in arrival order. A file format can use fixed-size records, an index, or offsets into variable-length data. The format must define byte ordering, field widths, and bounds independently of a compiler’s in-memory structure layout. Seeking past the end does not itself write intervening bytes. Subsequent writes can extend the file according to filesystem semantics. A robust parser checks offsets and lengths against the actual file size before accessing a region, using subtraction-based bounds checks that avoid overflowing offset + length .

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

13. File position
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
An open file description maintains a current file offset for interfaces such as read , write , and lseek on seekable objects. Descriptors created by dup or inherited through fork can refer to the same open file description and therefore share that offset. Separate open calls generally create separate open file descriptions, even when the pathname identifies the same file. Their current offsets are independent. Positional I/O such as pread and pwrite specifies an offset for an operation without using the shared current position in the same way, making it useful for independent random access.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

14. Metadata
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Metadata describes properties such as type, size, permissions, ownership, and timestamps. Descriptor-based inspection identifies the already-open object. A metadata result is a snapshot, not a lock that prevents later changes by another process. Security-sensitive code should avoid checking a pathname and then assuming the checked property remains true during a later open. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use problem. Use interfaces and ownership rules that bind validation to the actual object being used, and account for concurrent modification when the application permits it.

DO

15. Record boundaries without overflow
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Suppose a file format begins with a 16-byte header followed by fixed 24-byte records. A file of 160 bytes contains (160 - 16) / 24 = 6 complete records, with no trailing bytes. Record 4, using zero-based indexing, begins at 16 + 4 × 24 = 112 and occupies bytes 112 through 135. A safe validation sequence first requires file_size >= header_size . It then computes payload_size = file_size - header_size , verifies that payload_size % record_size == 0 , and derives the record count. Only after checking index < record_count should it form the selected record’s offset. For an arbitrary byte range with offset o and length n , prefer: This avoids computing an unchecked sum that could wrap. The checks establish a valid range in the observed file size; they do not prevent another process from truncating the file afterward. The application needs an immutability or coordination policy when concurrent modification is possible.

16. Sequential versus random file access
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
Reading a 1 MiB file from beginning to end advances the file offset naturally after each read. To revisit byte 100 without rereading earlier bytes, a seekable regular file can use lseek to reposition before reading. Pipes and terminals are streams and generally do not support arbitrary seek semantics.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

17. Metadata is not file content
Systems mechanisms and source lecture

SAY
A file’s permissions, owner, timestamps, and size are metadata. Reading file data does not automatically reveal all metadata, and changing metadata does not necessarily change file bytes. Systems code often uses separate interfaces such as stat to query this information.

In plain English: The program asks the operating system to move bytes to or from a resource, much like using a numbered ticket to ask a clerk for the right item.

21. Subtraction protects a range check from overflow
Reason about the implementation

SAY
For an arbitrary slice, the tempting test offset plus length less than or equal to size can fail when that addition wraps. Instead first establish that offset is no greater than the size. Then compare length with size minus offset, which is now safe to form. For a five-byte file, offset five and length zero describes an empty range at the end; offset six is invalid even for zero length. These checks are about the observed size. They do not stop another process from truncating the file after validation. The application must either hold a stable input or handle changes under an explicit coordination policy.

DO
Ask learners to classify the two empty-range boundary cases.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.014 · Worked example — Record boundaries without overflow

------------------------------------------------------------

22. Metadata describes the object; it does not lock it
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A size of one hundred in a metadata result does not freeze the file at one hundred bytes. Another permitted writer can change it afterward. Likewise, checking a pathname's permissions and later opening that path leaves time for the namespace entry to change. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. Descriptor-based inspection helps bind the check to the object actually opened, but it does not magically prevent all concurrent mutations. State the ownership and synchronization policy: perhaps inputs are immutable during parsing, or the reader detects and rejects inconsistent content. A security-sensitive design needs both object identity and a clear plan for changes after inspection.

DO
Separate namespace replacement from modification of the same object.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.012 · 33.5 Metadata

------------------------------------------------------------

23. Logical length need not equal allocated storage
Reason about the implementation

SAY
A file can have a large logical length without allocating physical storage for every region. Sparse-file behavior is one reason size and storage consumption differ. Seeking beyond the end changes the position; it does not by itself fill the gap with an application write. The format must also define its byte representation independently of a C++ structure's in-memory layout. Padding, byte order, and field width can vary across builds. Saving sizeof a struct and calling that a stable record format creates a hidden compiler dependency. An explicit format gives the reader enough information to validate offsets and decode fields consistently.

DO
Ask which parts of a record must be specified in bytes.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.008 · 33.3 Random-access files

------------------------------------------------------------

24. Copied descriptors may share position; separate opens need not
Reason about the implementation

SAY
Suppose two descriptors share one open file description. Reading two bytes through the first advances the position seen through the second. Copying or duplicating a handle does not necessarily create an independent cursor through the file. By contrast, separate open operations usually have distinct open descriptions and positions even if the underlying file is the same. This distinction explains surprising interleaved reads in larger programs. If independent random access is required, choose positional operations or independent open descriptions rather than surrounding every read with an unprotected seek. The invariant is about which shared object owns the mutable offset, not about how many integer variables appear in the code.

DO
Draw two descriptor entries pointing to one position-owning object.

28. Files are byte sequences, not implicit records
Code, diagrams, and debugging

SAY
Files are byte sequences, not implicit records. Check the starting position first, then subtract it from the size. Short-circuit && prevents an unsigned subtraction underflow from being used as a false large capacity.

A file model contains AB followed by CDE. Read three bytes beginning at byte offset 2.

Offsets here count bytes starting from zero. Subtraction after checking offset avoids an overflowing offset + count check. Any record boundaries come from a format layered over the bytes.

Check the starting position first, then subtract it from the size. Short-circuit && prevents an unsigned subtraction underflow from being used as a false large capacity.

substr extracts three characters starting at offset two, giving CDE. Strings can represent byte ranges; the operation does not infer application record boundaries.

The offset and requested count lie within the valid byte sequence. The subtraction is performed only after the offset fits.

A file size does not say where a logical record begins or whether its contents are valid for the format. In the extended lab: Treat an empty returned string as failure. A valid zero-length slice then becomes indistinguishable from rejection.

39. Chapter summary and maintenance
Recall and transfer

SAY
The slice owns its returned characters, so it does not depend on the original string’s later lifetime. The checks use the valid input extent, not its allocation capacity. An optional empty string is a success, while an empty optional is rejection. Real file reads can also fail or return fewer bytes; this memory model isolates the bounds contract.

Choose a simpler approach when its narrower contract is enough. Line-based text is convenient for simple human-readable records; fixed-width or indexed formats support different access needs.

When this system changes, retain a check that exposes the known failure: Treat an empty returned string as failure. A valid zero-length slice then becomes indistinguishable from rejection. Represent the success state separately from its data. Test the boundary at exactly end and just beyond end.

40. Design the parser around failure boundaries
Recall and transfer

SAY
A robust record reader has more than one validation step. It first validates the declared format and arithmetic. It then performs the operation and checks how many bytes actually arrived. A previously observed file size is not proof that the transfer completed. Keep errors distinct: malformed trailing bytes, an invalid record index, a short transfer, and an I/O error deserve different explanations. That makes a failed import diagnosable without exposing irrelevant implementation details. Tests should include a header-only file, an incomplete final record, an end-range request, and a large requested length that would overflow a naive sum. The tests protect the contract when the parser evolves.

DO
Choose one arithmetic failure and one I/O failure to test separately.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.014 · Worked example — Record boundaries without overflow

------------------------------------------------------------

41. Recall the four questions before reading bytes
Recall and transfer

SAY
Before a file operation, ask which object the program has opened, whether that endpoint supports the required operation, where the bytes will come from, and how the range remains valid. A regular file, a pipe, and a buffered stream can answer those questions differently even though all carry bytes. The fixed-record model explains safe addressing; the pread example explains independent positioning. Neither proves that an outside writer cannot change the file. Maintaining systems code means keeping those assumptions beside the operation so later developers do not turn a stable-input parser into a concurrent reader without adding the missing coordination and failure tests.

DO
Ask learners to describe one read without using the vague phrase open the file.

SOURCE
content/systems-programming/ch33.json → SP33.004 · 33.1 Regular files
